text: Lessons 17 and 18 built a real path between clouds and a way to resolve names across it. This lesson is about what actually happens when traffic uses that path for real — starting with latency, and then the cost that genuinely shapes multi-cloud architecture decisions: egress.

Two services in the same Azure region talk over infrastructure Microsoft fully controls end to end. Two services split across Azure and AWS talk over a link that leaves one cloud's network and enters another's — more hops, and hops neither cloud's SLA fully covers alone. A gateway-to-gateway VPN adds the most variability, since it still rides the public internet between the two gateway endpoints. A colocation meet-point is more predictable because it stays on private infrastructure, but it's still categorically different from same-region traffic. A design that assumes otherwise, hopping clouds two or three times per request, feels that latency directly in response time.

Then there's cost, and it's genuinely asymmetric. Both Azure and AWS price data transfer the same basic shape: moving data into a cloud from outside is typically free, moving data out is metered and billed per gigabyte. From either cloud's point of view, the other cloud is just an external network, so that asymmetry applies in full to cross-cloud traffic — a response AWS sends back to Azure is AWS egress, billed on AWS's side, regardless of how the link was built. Direction matters, not just total bytes moved.

That's why a chatty, bidirectional pattern — fetch a record from AWS, enrich it in Azure, write the result back, log a status update — is the most expensive possible way to use a cross-cloud link: egress gets charged on every outbound-crossing leg, multiplied by how often that pattern repeats. Real designs respond by minimizing cross-cloud round trips per request, batching instead of calling repeatedly, and caching locally in the calling cloud rather than re-fetching on every request.

It also informs where a service should actually run: when its heaviest-volume callers sit in one cloud and its data lives in the other, placing the service near its caller keeps the high-frequency traffic local and pushes the cross-cloud leg to the lower-frequency side — a periodic sync instead of a per-request lookup. Not the only input into placement, but ignoring it is how a cross-cloud design quietly outgrows its budget. Next: what happens when one of those two clouds has a bad day.
